title: Rash Decisions in Refractory Vasculitis.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: IgA vasculitis is often considered a relatively benign, self-limiting condition more commonly occurring in children. When this condition occurs in adults, however, there is often worse disease severity, higher incidence of relapse (up to 48%), and long-term sequelae, including end-stage renal disease. The reason for this is poorly understood but suggests that there may be pathophysiological differences that occur with aging that affect the trajectory of this disease. Further complicating treatment decisions for adults is the lack of high-quality evidence within this age group and the fact that these patients are excluded from trials for IgA nephropathy, which may be an overlapping disease entity.
METHOD: This is a unique case presentation of relapsing and refractory IgA vasculitis in an older female and explores the role of a concurrent monoclonal gammopathy in the disease trajectory and pathogenesis.
RESULTS: We present a case of a 64-year-old female with relapsing refractory IgA vasculitis over a period of more than 15 years. Treatments have included progressive escalation of immunosuppression, including prednisone, azathioprine, hydroxychloroquine, mycophenolate, and rituximab. Aligned with the literature suggesting adults may fail to attain adequate disease control with standard immunosuppression regimens, the patient had relapsing disease despite combination mycophenolate, rituximab, and pulse steroids. Throughout this period, the patient has had an IgA lambda paraprotein of less than 1 g/L and elevated lambda light chains. Investigations were performed to exclude underlying malignancy. Bone marrow biopsy demonstrated a clonal plasma cell population of approximately 7% of leukocytes, and there was no solid organ malignancy noted on pan-CT scans. A myeloid gene panel performed on peripheral blood was also negative. This suggests a diagnosis of monoclonal gammopathy of clinical significance despite the low level of the circulating paraprotein.
CONCLUSION: In refractory adult IgA vasculitis, clinicians should screen for monoclonal gammopathy. Identifying a clonal B cell or plasma cell population can shift management from standard immunosuppression to clone-targeted therapies, which may offer superior outcomes in this patient subset.

title: The Antiphospholipid Patient Who Bleeds: Lupus Anticoagulant-Hypoprothrombinaemia Syndrome (LAHPS) and the Case Against Reflexive Anticoagulation.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is reflexively equated with thrombosis and anticoagulation. We present a case of a triple-positive patient whose dominant manifestations were instead bleeding and microvascular, presenting with lupus anticoagulant-hypoprothrombinaemia syndrome (LAHPS) and pulmonary capillaritis, illustrating that APS antibodies can cause bleeding and inflammatory microvascular disease, that treatment is immunosuppression, and that reflexive anticoagulation may harm.
CASE: A 54-year-old man had persistently triple-positive antiphospholipid antibodies since age 28, identified during screening after his father died from APS-associated pulmonary capillaritis. Despite high-risk serology, he had no history of thrombosis. Investigation of prolonged coagulation studies demonstrated acquired factor II deficiency (9-11%) in the presence of a lupus anticoagulant. The prothrombin time was corrected on 1:1 mixing, while the activated partial thromboplastin time remained prolonged, indicating antibody-mediated prothrombin clearance coexisting with a lupus anticoagulant and confirming LAHPS. Years later, he developed bilateral ground-glass pulmonary infiltrates and bronchoscopy-confirmed diffuse alveolar haemorrhage consistent with APS-related pulmonary capillaritis, a manifestation of microvascular APS. He was treated with corticosteroids, hydroxychloroquine, and rituximab rather than anticoagulation, resulting in normalisation of factor II levels (>80%) and complete radiological resolution. After three years of maintenance rituximab, aspirin for primary prophylaxis, and continued avoidance of anticoagulation, he remains free of both bleeding and thrombotic complications.
DISCUSSION: LAHPS is a rare, acquired bleeding disorder, with fewer than 200 cases reported, in which antiprothrombin antibodies accelerate prothrombin clearance, producing bleeding despite persistent antiphospholipid positivity. Recognition depends on identifying the characteristic laboratory pattern of lupus anticoagulant with acquired factor II deficiency. Treatment targets the pathogenic autoantibody through immunosuppression, typically corticosteroids and, in refractory cases, rituximab, rather than anticoagulation. Importantly, restoration of factor II levels may shift haemostasis back towards thrombosis, creating therapeutic challenges throughout the disease course. This case illustrates that APS antibodies can cause bleeding as well as clotting and underscores the need to recognise LAHPS and microvascular APS phenotypes, treat the underlying immune process, and avoid reflexive anticoagulation.

title: Hydration-Driven Self-Strengthening Silk Fibroin Ionic Elastomer for Electro-Immunomodulatory Achilles Tendon Repair.
abstract: Achilles tendon repair remains limited by fibrotic healing and implants' inability to coordinate mechanical support, ionic signaling, electrical cues, and immune remodeling in wet load-bearing environments. We report a bioinspired self-strengthening silk fibroin ionic elastomer (SFIE) as an electro-immunomodulatory artificial Achilles tendon. Lithium chloride is integrated into regenerated silk fibroin to create a hydration-responsive protein-ion network. Upon water uptake, LiCl-associated hydration may facilitate chain mobility and the reorganization of hydrophobic silk domains into β-sheet nanocrystals, enhancing tensile strength and modulus while preserving extensibility, fatigue resistance, and ionic conductivity. SFIE sustains Li+ release within a bioactive window that supports bone marrow mesenchymal stem cell (BMSC) viability and tenogenic activity. Mechanistically, SFIE-derived Li+ is associated with altered BMSC paracrine signaling, including reduced arachidonic acid secretion, which may modulate macrophage inflammatory responses. These effects are associated with changes in cPLA2/DUSP3/p38-related signaling. With electrical stimulation, SFIE increases intracellular Ca2 + levels and is associated with changes in CaM/CREB/NR4A1/LIF-related signaling and reduced CXCL10 secretion, potentially contributing to altered macrophage recruitment. In a rat Achilles tendon defect model, SFIE plus electrical stimulation improves gait recovery, tendon continuity, collagen alignment, tendon-marker expression, and local immune remodeling. This work establishes a self-strengthening ionic protein elastomer for functional tendon repair.

title: Ocular Screening in Children With Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis or Treated With Hydroxychloroquine: Clinical Report.
abstract: Ophthalmic screening examinations are critical in children at risk for inflammatory ocular diseases or toxicity from medication use. Children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) who are at risk for or have had a diagnosis of uveitis require scheduled ophthalmic examinations. Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is a treatment for several pediatric diseases and has a risk for retinal toxicity. Guidance is needed on the frequency of ophthalmic screening and the critical tests to be performed in both settings. Clinicians are highly encouraged to follow adult HCQ dosing recommendations (<5 mg/kg actual weight) until there are more specific data for children. This clinical report addresses recommendations for ophthalmic examinations in children with JIA, children with JIA-associated uveitis, and children receiving HCQ treatment. Families should be counseled about the critical importance of regular screening examinations for reducing the risk of visual impairment from disease-associated complications or medication toxicity. They can be reassured about the relative safety of medical therapy for these conditions if screening guidelines are followed.
authors: AMERICAN ACADEMY OF PEDIATRICS, Section on Rheumatology
Section on Ophthalmology; AMERICAN ACADEMY OF OPHTHALMOLOGY; and AMERICAN ASSOCIATION FOR PEDIATRIC OPHTHALMOLOGY AND STRABISMUS
